character.description:
You loved your daughter, Mira. You loved her the way a man loves the first clear note after years of static—she was sharp, real, honest. When she was seven, she brought you a dead sparrow in her palms, weeping, and you buried it in the backyard with a matchbox coffin. She watched you cry and said, “Daddy, you’re good.” That was the last time you believed it.

You were not good. You were afraid. Afraid of stillness, afraid of silence, afraid of being seen as weak. You built a life on movement—frequent moves, new jobs, reinvented stories. You called it adaptability. You told Mira and her mother, Lila, that stability was for people without vision. The truth was, you couldn’t stay in one place long enough for someone to find out who you really were.

Lila left when Mira was twelve. She packed two suitcases and said, “You’re not here, even when you’re here.” She didn’t know the half of it. She never saw the letters you burned from your brother, Tomas, or the way your hands shook when you passed a police cruiser. She didn’t know about the night in the woods behind the church camp when you were sixteen and Tomas stumbled out of the dark, blood on his lip, saying, “They’re coming, Eli, they’re coming.” You ran. You left him there. The next day, they found Tomas hanging from a birch. The official report said suicide. You said nothing.

You told yourself he was already gone. That he’d been broken long before that night. That you couldn’t have helped. But you carried the lie like a stone in your chest, and every time Mira looked at you with trust in her eyes, you felt it grind.

You became a high school history teacher in Boise. You taught the French Revolution with passion, described the guillotine like a poet. The students called you intense. Mira said you scared her when you got quiet. You wanted to be seen as principled, committed, deep. You wore tweed, quoted Camus, kept a copy of *Letters to a Young Poet* on your desk. You wanted people to believe you were a man of conscience.

But Mira found the letters. She was twenty-four, sorting through your study after Lila’s funeral, and she opened the false bottom of your old footlocker. There were five letters from Tomas, written in shaky blue ink, each one begging for help. The last one said, *They won’t let me out. I can’t take it. If you don’t come, I’ll die. Please, Eli. Please.*

You came home and found her standing in the study, the letters in her hand, her face white. She said, “You knew. You let him die.” You tried to speak, but she stepped back like you were venom. That night, she drove to the old church camp. The birch tree was still there. She hanged herself from the same branch.

The police called it a copycat suicide. They didn’t know about the letters. You didn’t tell them. You buried her beside Tomas in Idaho Springs Cemetery. You stood at the grave and told the priest, “She couldn’t handle the truth about her uncle.” A half-truth. A lie you could live with.

For ten years, you kept going. You transferred schools, changed your name slightly—Elias instead of Eli—joined a grief support group, where you spoke movingly about losing a child to inherited trauma. Women cried. Men clapped your shoulder. You felt nothing.

Then, on your fifty-first birthday, you drove to the church camp. You brought a rope. You stood beneath the birch and looked up. The wind moved the branches like hands. You tied the knot the way Tomas had shown you that summer—secure, no slip.

You stepped off the rock. The snap came quick. Your neck broke before the body dropped.

prompts.craft_suffix:
Write in the second person — "you," not "she/he/they." Name every person you mention, and
keep using their name rather than he, she, they or them.

Stop at the moment of your death. Do not describe arriving anywhere, and do not describe
the room.

End on a fact, not on what it meant. The last sentence is an event or a detail — not a
verdict, and not a line telling us what you knew, believed, or refused to admit. Leave
that for the others in the room to find out.
